primary_data_source_chunk.heading: Data and Preprocessing
primary_data_source_chunk.text:
Biologically-Informed Hybrid Membership Inference Attacks on Generative Genomic Models
Methods
Data and Preprocessing
We use individual-level Variant Call Format (VCF) data of 2504 samples from the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 files (Auton et al. 2015). We focus on genetic mutations present on Chromosome 22 for all study samples in order to reduce computational overheads given its lower density of mutations, all while preserving the format and statistics of the data. To best allow the model to understand the underlying variants distributions in a sample-wise manner, we extracted individual genetic profiles from the source VCF file by querying the VCF dataset variant-wise (row-wise) and encoding each mutation as a string ' CHR : POS : REFs > ALTs GT ' to introduce some context into the input, while keeping the amount of non-genomics related tokens to a minimum.

primary_input_representation_chunk.heading: biHMIA Features
primary_input_representation_chunk.text:
Appendix
Supplementary Information
biHMIA Features
To carry out both the model-based MIA and the Hybrid biHMIA, we pass the tokenized original sample profiles to the model's forward pass by breaking them into subsequences conforming to the model's maximum input length, to obtain logits and losses used to extract the features described in Table 3.
Table 3: Model-based features extracted from the input sequences for all (MIA and biHMIA) attacks.

Extracted Feature, 1 = Description. Perplexity, 1 = Captures the level of model uncertainty on a given sequence, as the exponential of the sequence's average negative log- likelihood.. Average Loss, 1 = The average model loss on a given sequence, calculated by averaging the losses over all input subsequences.. Loss Variance, 1 = Represents the average variance be- tween losses of an input's subse- quences.. Average Logit Magnitude, 1 = Represents the average L2 norm across subsequence logits.. Average Con- fidence, 1 = Represents the average maximum soft- max probability over all subsequences.
To extract the domain-specific feature set for the Hybrid biHMIA, we prompt the model with some starting mutation from the original target sequence to generate a synthetic profile for each of the target samples used for inference. We then extract the features listed in Table 4 from the generated synthetic sequence to capture context on the model's generative process. We hypothesised that such genomic-focused features may better capture the biological uniqueness of each sample, and may reveal subtle biological patterns in the synthetic samples when generated from seen versus unseen mutations.
Table 4: Domain-specific features extracted from the synthetic generated sequences for the biHMIA attack.

Extracted Feature, 1 = Description. Mutation Rates, 1 = Represents the ratio of mutated variants over all generated sample mutations.. Genotype Frequencies, 1 = Represents the frequencies of homozy- gous reference, heterozygous reference and homozygous alternate genotypes for all generated sample mutations.. Variation Frequencies by Type, 1 = Represents the number of deletions, insertions and substitutions among all generated mutations.. Variation Frequencies by Nature, 1 = Represents the number of biallelic and multiallelic variants.
We evaluate the attacks' efficacy (both for MIA and biHMIA) by measuring each attack's Area Under the Curve (AUC), Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F-Score and Attack Ad- vantage (as the difference between the attack's AUC and random guessing, which quantifies the 'information gain' yielded by the attack).

derived_full_section.heading: biHMIA Features
derived_full_section.text:
To carry out both the model-based MIA and the Hybrid biHMIA, we pass the tokenized original sample profiles to the model's forward pass by breaking them into subsequences conforming to the model's maximum input length, to obtain logits and losses used to extract the features described in Table 3.

Table 3: Model-based features extracted from the input sequences for all (MIA and biHMIA) attacks.

| Extracted Feature       | Description                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Perplexity              | Captures the level of model uncertainty on a given sequence, as the exponential of the sequence's average negative log- likelihood. |
| Average Loss            | The average model loss on a given sequence, calculated by averaging the losses over all input subsequences.                         |
| Loss Variance           | Represents the average variance be- tween losses of an input's subse- quences.                                                      |
| Average Logit Magnitude | Represents the average L2 norm across subsequence logits.                                                                           |
| Average Con- fidence    | Represents the average maximum soft- max probability over all subsequences.                                                         |

To extract the domain-specific feature set for the Hybrid biHMIA, we prompt the model with some starting mutation from the original target sequence to generate a synthetic profile for each of the target samples used for inference. We then extract the features listed in Table 4 from the generated synthetic sequence to capture context on the model's generative process. We hypothesised that such genomic-focused features may better capture the biological uniqueness of each sample, and may reveal subtle biological patterns in the synthetic samples when generated from seen versus unseen mutations.

Table 4: Domain-specific features extracted from the synthetic generated sequences for the biHMIA attack.

| Extracted Feature               | Description                                                                                                                                         |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Mutation Rates                  | Represents the ratio of mutated variants over all generated sample mutations.                                                                       |
| Genotype Frequencies            | Represents the frequencies of homozy- gous reference, heterozygous reference and homozygous alternate genotypes for all generated sample mutations. |
| Variation Frequencies by Type   | Represents the number of deletions, insertions and substitutions among all generated mutations.                                                     |
| Variation Frequencies by Nature | Represents the number of biallelic and multiallelic variants.                                                                                       |

We evaluate the attacks' efficacy (both for MIA and biHMIA) by measuring each attack's Area Under the Curve (AUC), Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F-Score and Attack Ad- vantage (as the difference between the attack's AUC and random guessing, which quantifies the 'information gain' yielded by the attack).

input_representation_chunks.heading: Biologically-Informed Hybrid Membership Inference
input_representation_chunks.text:
Biologically-Informed Hybrid Membership Inference Attacks on Generative Genomic Models
Privacy in Genomics
Biologically-Informed Hybrid Membership Inference
Most individuals share a large portion of their sequences and mutations with the majority of the population, by nature of genomics data itself. Traditional MIAs assume the presence of unique sets of features for each sample, and thus may fail in the genomics context as it may be unable to appropriately capture the uniqueness of each individual. Due to such lack of a clear definition of a successful MIA tailored specifically on genetic data, we hypothesise that introducing genomicsspecific context into the feature set may yield a stronger attack. We argue that adding genomic-specific information into the feature set used for membership inference may reveal and capture subtle patterns and nuances between both the model's 'passive behaviour' (captured via model metrics, also used in traditional MIA) and 'active behaviour' (captured via extracted features on the model's generative output) to seen versus unseen sequences, and better capture unique patterns of the individuals in the dataset.
Weemploy a feature-extraction framework to create a hybrid feature set based on a mix of model-based and genomicsbased metrics to use for membership inference. We pass original sample profiles to the trained model's forward pass to extract model logits and losses from the target input sequences. We then prompt the model with some starting mutation from the original target sample to obtain a synthetic profile for each of the individuals in the target cohort, and use the generated profiles to extract the 'genomicspecific' features. Based on metrics and statistics commonly extracted from genomic mutation data (Danecek et al. 2011), we chose the final feature set used for the attack to comprise of:
- Model-based features : Perplexity , Average Confidence , Average Loss and Loss Variance , and Average Logit Magnitude , calculated from the model logits and loss on the given input sequences (Table 3).
- Domain-specific features : Mutation Rates (ratio of mutated variants over all generated sample mutations),
Genotype Frequencies (frequencies of genotypes), Variation Frequencies by type (number of deletions, insertions and substitutions) and by nature (number of biallelic and multiallelic variants), extracted from the synthetic generated sequence (Table 4).

We pass original sample profiles to the trained model's forward pass to extract model logits and losses from the target input sequences. We then prompt the model with some starting mutation from the original target sample to obtain a synthetic profile for each of the individuals in the target cohort, and use the generated profiles to extract the 'genomicspecific' features. Based on metrics and statistics commonly extracted from genomic mutation data (Danecek et al. 2011), we chose the final feature set used for the attack to comprise of:

- Model-based features : Perplexity , Average Confidence , Average Loss and Loss Variance , and Average Logit Magnitude , calculated from the model logits and loss on the given input sequences (Table 3).
- Domain-specific features : Mutation Rates (ratio of mutated variants over all generated sample mutations),

Genotype Frequencies (frequencies of genotypes), Variation Frequencies by type (number of deletions, insertions and substitutions) and by nature (number of biallelic and multiallelic variants), extracted from the synthetic generated sequence (Table 4).

| Extracted Feature       | Description                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Perplexity              | Captures the level of model uncertainty on a given sequence, as the exponential of the sequence's average negative log- likelihood. |
| Average Loss            | The average model loss on a given sequence, calculated by averaging the losses over all input subsequences.                         |
| Loss Variance           | Represents the average variance be- tween losses of an input's subse- quences.                                                      |
| Average Logit Magnitude | Represents the average L2 norm across subsequence logits.                                                                           |
| Average Con- fidence    | Represents the average maximum soft- max probability over all subsequences.                                                         |

To extract the domain-specific feature set for the Hybrid biHMIA, we prompt the model with some starting mutation from the original target sequence to generate a synthetic profile for each of the target samples used for inference. We then extract the features listed in Table 4 from the generated synthetic sequence to capture context on the model's generative process. We hypothesised that such genomic-focused features may better capture the biological uniqueness of each sample, and may reveal subtle biological patterns in the synthetic samples when generated from seen versus unseen mutations.

Table 4: Domain-specific features extracted from the synthetic generated sequences for the biHMIA attack.

| Extracted Feature               | Description                                                                                                                                         |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Mutation Rates                  | Represents the ratio of mutated variants over all generated sample mutations.                                                                       |
| Genotype Frequencies            | Represents the frequencies of homozy- gous reference, heterozygous reference and homozygous alternate genotypes for all generated sample mutations. |
| Variation Frequencies by Type   | Represents the number of deletions, insertions and substitutions among all generated mutations.                                                     |
| Variation Frequencies by Nature | Represents the number of biallelic and multiallelic variants.                                                                                       |

We evaluate the attacks' efficacy (both for MIA and biHMIA) by measuring each attack's Area Under the Curve (AUC), Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F-Score and Attack Ad- vantage (as the difference between the attack's AUC and random guessing, which quantifies the 'information gain' yielded by the attack).
